items.why_watch: If you've seen Casper Kelly's 'Too Many Cooks' and wondered what he'd do with a feature-length canvas, this breakdown makes a strong case that 'Buddy' rewards close attention. Lucas Blue walks through specific symbols and structural choices rather than just summarizing the plot, so it functions as a genuine companion piece rather than a recap. Worth watching before or after the film if you're drawn to horror-comedy that embeds psychological subtext in domestic settings.

reading_room.title: Not-Writing
reading_room.snippet: by TJ Price I haven’t been writing lately. I’m fully aware that sometimes there are cycles to these things; that there’s no sense in feeling guilt or shame about it—and yet. An author said once in an interview that if they went too long without writing, they “turned into a bit of a jackass.” I…
reading_room.blurb: TJ Price sits with the quiet dread of a writing life gone silent and asks what it costs — not professionally, but personally — when the words stop coming and you slowly start to recognize the person you're becoming without them.

reading_room.title: As AI Lay Dying: Analog Adventures in the Old South
reading_room.snippet: by Sean Murphy i. While there is much to admire and recommend in the excellent documentary Jiro Dreams of Sushi, especially for young creatives or academics who want to better understand–and appreciate–mastery and what it involves and requires, there’s one sequence that has stayed with me. The apprentice chefs are on rice duty before they even…
reading_room.blurb: Sean Murphy uses the rice-polishing apprentices of *Jiro Dreams of Sushi* as a doorway into a deeper question: what gets lost when we outsource the slow, unglamorous labor of mastery to machines that can only simulate having earned it.

reading_room.title: Long Before Toy Story, It-Narratives Imagined the Inner Lives of Objects
reading_room.snippet: It’s nighttime in the playroom and the toys have gathered for a conference. For modern audiences, this scene likely evokes the imaginative world of Toy Story, the long-running film franchise about the secret lives of children’s toys, which launched to
reading_room.blurb: Long before Pixar, eighteenth-century writers were giving coins, corsets, and carriages an inner life — this piece recovers the strange, playful literary genre that first dared to ask what the world looks like from the perspective of a thing.

reading_room.title: What being a moderate means to me
reading_room.snippet: Matt Lutz at Humean Being: It often seems that there is no more despised creature than the political moderate. “Moderate,” and its synonym “centrist,” are often used as terms of abuse. The moderate, in the popular political imagination, is wishy-washy, an inveterate hair-splitter who stands for nothing, the kind of collaborator who would say that…
reading_room.blurb: Matt Lutz mounts a quiet, careful defense of political moderation — not as the absence of conviction, but as a distinct and demanding intellectual stance that refuses the comfort of certainty at either extreme.

news.title: Kismet, London SE1: ‘The sort of beans that make you want to move to the sun’ – restaurant review
news.snippet: The first genuinely cool thing to have happened in Borough Market for ages A Turkish-Cypriot meyhane , which translates roughly as “wine house”, has slotted in upstairs at the Globe Tavern in Borough Market , south London. Any cab driver worth his salt will bend your ear over the fact that this is “where Bridget Jones lives”, which might be a bit confusing if you’ve booked in to eat kuzu şiş (lamb neck kebabs) and to knock back a couple of rakis with a fermented turnip juice chaser. That Bridget Jones trivia, by the way, is completely true: the upstairs space at the Globe was used as the heroine’s gaff in that famous film franchise.
news.blurb: A Turkish-Cypriot wine house tucked above a Borough Market pub, serving beans so sun-drenched they've apparently earned their own passport — a restaurant review worth savouring.
